q: Dr. Bunsen buys a used lab centrifuge from a scientific-equipment dealer. The salesperson tells him: (1) "This is a fantastic machine; you'll love it," and (2) "It spins at 15,000 RPM." The centrifuge tops out at 9,000 RPM. Which statement created an express warranty?
o: Both statements.
Only statement (1).
Neither, because the centrifuge was sold used.
Neither, because the statements were oral rather than written.
Only statement (2).
oe: Statement (1) is general praise. Puffing doesn't create a warranty under § 2-313(2).
Statement (1) is the puffing; statement (2) is the warranty.
Express warranties apply to used goods just as to new ones.
§ 2-313 requires no writing. Oral affirmations of fact can be express warranties.

Correct. A specific, measurable affirmation of fact about the goods is an express warranty (§ 2-313(1)(a)). "Fantastic" and "you'll love it" are opinion and commendation, which create no warranty (§ 2-313(2)).
topic: 3 · Express warranties (§ 2-313) — Fact vs. puffing

q: A used-equipment dealer sells Gordon a 12-year-old lawn tractor for a low price. Two days later, the engine seizes during ordinary mowing. The contract has no disclaimer. Which statement is most accurate?
o: No implied warranty arises, because the tractor was sold used.
The dealer warranted that the tractor would perform as well as a new one.
The warranty applies only if the dealer knew the engine was about to fail.
No implied warranty arises, because the price was low.
The merchantability warranty applies but is measured by what's appropriate for a tractor of that age and price, and an engine that seizes in two days may still breach it.
oe: Used goods sold by a merchant still carry the warranty, though its content is reduced.
The warranty for used goods is reduced; the buyer can't expect new-goods quality.
Implied warranties are strict; the seller's knowledge of the defect is irrelevant.
Price is evidence of the quality promised, but a low price doesn't eliminate the warranty.

Correct. A merchant's sale of used goods carries a merchantability warranty with a reduced content appropriate to second-hand goods (§ 2-314 cmt. 3). Even a cheap old tractor should run for more than two days.
topic: 4 · Implied warranties (§§ 2-314, 2-315) — Used goods: reduced warranty

q: Fozzie sells 500 rubber chickens to Gonzo for $8,000, payment due in 30 days. The signed contract says: "Seller may not assign its right to payment, and any attempted assignment is void." Fozzie assigns the right to payment to Muppet Bank, which sends Gonzo a signed notice telling him to pay the bank. Gonzo pays Fozzie anyway, and the bank sues Gonzo. What is the most likely result?
o: Gonzo wins, because he paid the full price to the party he actually contracted with.
The bank wins, because a term restricting assignment of a right to payment for goods is ineffective, and after notice Gonzo could discharge his debt only by paying the bank.
Gonzo wins, because the contract expressly made any attempted assignment void.
The bank wins, but Fozzie is liable to Gonzo for breaching the anti-assignment clause.
The bank wins, but only if Gonzo consented to the assignment in a signed record.
oe: After notification, paying the assignor does not discharge the obligor (§ 9-406(a)). Gonzo may have to pay twice and seek repayment from Fozzie.
Correct. § 9-406(d) overrides the anti-assignment term for an account (a right to payment for goods sold), and under § 9-406(a) payment to the assignor after notice does not discharge the buyer.
The "void" language would matter for most rights, but § 9-406(d) makes it ineffective as to a right to payment for goods.
§ 9-406(d) provides that such an assignment is not a breach or default, so Gonzo has no claim against Fozzie for making it.
The account debtor's consent is not required for an assignment of a right to payment.
topic: 1 · Assignment & delegation (§ 2-210) — Void clause vs. right to payment

q: Telly buys a used e-bike from Oscar's Resale under a contract stating: "SOLD AS IS, WITH ALL FAULTS." The e-bike turns out to be stolen, and the true owner reclaims it. Telly sues Oscar's Resale. What is the most likely result?
o: Oscar's wins, because Telly could have checked the bike's ownership before buying.
Oscar's wins, because Telly bought used goods.
Telly wins, because "as is" language does not disclaim the warranty of title.
Oscar's wins, because "as is" excludes all warranties.
Telly wins, but only if Oscar's knew the bike was stolen.
oe: The buyer has no duty to investigate title; the seller warrants it.
Every seller warrants title, whether the goods are new or used.

Correct. The title warranty can be excluded only by specific language or by circumstances giving the buyer reason to know the seller doesn't claim title (§ 2-312(2)). It isn't an "implied warranty" under § 2-316, so "as is" doesn't reach it (cmt. 6).
"As is" excludes implied warranties under § 2-316(3)(a). The title warranty isn't one of them.
The title warranty doesn't depend on the seller's knowledge.
topic: 5 · Warranty of title & infringement (§ 2-312) — "As is" and title

q: A contract for a commercial espresso machine says: "Seller will repair or replace any defective component within one year." Nothing else in the contract addresses remedies. The machine's boiler is defective. Instead of a repair, the buyer sues for damages. May it do so?
o: No, because a repair-or-replace clause is always the buyer's sole remedy.
No, unless the seller has first refused to repair the boiler.
No, because a remedy limitation need not be conspicuous to be enforced.
Yes, because the remedy wasn't expressly made exclusive.
Yes, but only for consequential damages, not direct damages.
oe: Only an expressly exclusive remedy is the sole remedy.
Refusal matters to failure of essential purpose. Here the agreed remedy was never exclusive in the first place.
True that conspicuousness isn't required, but the clause still had to be expressly exclusive to bar other remedies.

Correct. Resort to a remedy provided in the contract is optional unless the remedy is expressly agreed to be exclusive, in which case it is the sole remedy (§ 2-719(1)(b)). Exclusivity must be clearly expressed (cmt. 2).
The buyer has its full range of Article 2 remedies, direct and consequential.
topic: 8 · Limited remedies (§ 2-719) — Remedy not expressly exclusive

q: The Swedish Chef orders a set of hand-forged chef's knives from Beaker, a blacksmith whose distinctive forging technique is the reason the Chef chose him. The contract says nothing about delegation. Swamped with orders, Beaker hands the job to another smith whose knives are well regarded but made differently. May the Chef refuse the knives the other smith tenders?
o: No, because the other smith's knives are well regarded, so the Chef suffers no harm.
Yes, because the Chef has a substantial interest in having Beaker himself perform.
No, because a party may always delegate unless the contract expressly prohibits it.
No, because knives are goods, and § 2-210 bars delegation only in contracts for services.
Yes, but only if the Chef first demands and fails to receive adequate assurance from the other smith.
oe: The test isn't whether the substitute is competent. When the goods turn on the maker's personal skill, the buyer may insist on that maker.

Correct. Delegation is barred when the other party has a substantial interest in having the original promisor perform or control the acts required (§ 2-210(1)). A buyer of custom goods chosen for the maker's personal skill has that interest.
Contract language is one limit, but § 2-210(1) has a second one: the other party's substantial interest in the original promisor's performance.
§ 2-210 governs contracts for the sale of goods, and its substantial-interest limit applies to them.
A demand for assurance is available under § 2-210(6), but here the delegation itself is ineffective, so the Chef needn't take that step first.
topic: 1 · Assignment & delegation (§ 2-210) — Substantial interest: custom craft

q: Under § 2-718(1), a court tests whether a liquidated damages amount is reasonable in light of all of the following EXCEPT:
o: The harm the parties anticipated the breach would cause.
Whether the breaching party acted willfully.
The actual harm caused by the breach.
The inconvenience or nonfeasibility of otherwise obtaining an adequate remedy.
The difficulties of proving the loss.
oe: A statutory factor: reasonableness is judged "in the light of the anticipated or actual harm."

Correct. Willfulness isn't a factor. § 2-718(1) looks only to the anticipated or actual harm, the difficulty of proving loss, and the inconvenience or nonfeasibility of otherwise obtaining an adequate remedy.
A statutory factor: the test is anticipated or actual harm.
A statutory factor named in § 2-718(1).
A statutory factor named in § 2-718(1).
topic: 2 · Liquidated damages (§ 2-718) — Reasonableness factors

q: A state has adopted Alternative A of § 2-318. Gina buys a blender from a store, and its blade assembly flies off. Which injured person may sue the store for breach of warranty?
o: A houseguest injured while making smoothies in Gina's kitchen.
A friend whose expensive countertop was cracked, with no physical injury.
Gina's adult son, who lives across town, injured while using the blender in his own apartment.
A coworker injured when Gina brings the blender to an office party.
A neighbor who borrowed the blender and was injured in his own kitchen.
oe: Correct. Alternative A extends the seller's warranty to natural persons in the buyer's family or household and guests in the buyer's home, if it's reasonable to expect them to use or be affected by the goods and they are injured in person.
Alternative A covers only injury to the person.
He isn't a member of Gina's household or a guest in her home, so Alternative A doesn't reach him.
Alternative A doesn't reach people outside the buyer's family, household, or home.
The neighbor isn't in Gina's household and wasn't a guest in her home.
topic: 7 · Privity & cumulation (§§ 2-317, 2-318) — § 2-318 Alternative A: who's covered

q: A farm-equipment dealer tells Luis, "The baler's out back if you want to take a look." Luis says he's in a hurry and buys it without looking. A worn belt, obvious at a glance, soon snaps. Luis sues for breach of the implied warranty of merchantability. Does the examination exclusion of § 2-316(3)(b) defeat the claim?
o: Yes, because farm equipment is sold "as is" by usage of trade.
Yes, because the defect was obvious, so Luis must have known of it.
No, because examination can exclude only express warranties.
No; an invitation to look isn't a demand that the buyer examine the goods.
Yes, because Luis turned down the dealer's offer to examine the baler before buying it.
oe: Nothing in the facts shows such a usage of trade.
Obviousness matters only once the exclusion applies. Without an examination or a refusal after demand, it doesn't.
§ 2-316(3)(b) concerns implied warranties.

Correct. The exclusion applies when the buyer examined the goods or refused to examine them after the seller's demand that he do so (§ 2-316(3)(b), cmt. 8). An invitation to look isn't a demand, so Luis's warranty stands.
Declining a casual offer isn't the refusal § 2-316(3)(b) requires. The seller must demand a full examination.
topic: 6 · Warranty disclaimers (§ 2-316) — Examination: no demand

q: Statler contracts to buy $4,000 of theater seats from Waldorf's Seating. The contract says that if Statler cancels, he "shall pay Seller $40,000 as liquidated damages." Statler cancels before the seats are shipped, and Waldorf resells them with a $300 loss. What may Waldorf recover?
o: Only his actual damages, because the clause is void as a penalty.
$4,000, the full contract price, as the maximum a seller can ever liquidate.
A reduced, reasonable amount that the court sets in place of the $40,000.
$40,000, because Statler freely agreed to the amount.
Nothing, because a void penalty clause voids the entire contract.
oe: Correct. A term fixing unreasonably large liquidated damages is void as a penalty (§ 2-718(1)). Ten times the price bears no relation to any plausible harm, so Waldorf falls back on his ordinary remedies (e.g., § 2-706).
No rule caps liquidated damages at the price. The question is reasonableness, and this clause fails it.
§ 2-718(1) declares the term void. The court doesn't rewrite it; the seller proves actual damages instead.
Freedom of contract stops at penalties. § 2-718(1) voids unreasonably large liquidated damages.
Only the penalty term is void. The rest of the contract, including Waldorf's ordinary remedies, survives.
topic: 2 · Liquidated damages (§ 2-718) — Penalty: unreasonably large

q: Which of the following statements about assignment and delegation under UCC § 2-210 is NOT correct?
o: Absent a contrary agreement, a seller may delegate its duty to tender standard goods without the buyer's consent.
An assignment of "the contract" is generally both an assignment of rights and a delegation of duties.
A seller's right to payment can generally be assigned without the buyer's consent.
A clause barring assignment of "the contract" is generally read to bar only the delegation of duties.
Once the delegate agrees to perform, the delegating seller is discharged from liability for any breach.
oe: True. Delegation needs no consent unless the agreement bars it or the other party has a substantial interest in the original promisor's performance (§ 2-210(1)).
True. § 2-210(5) reads a general assignment of "the contract" as a delegation too, unless the language or circumstances show otherwise.
True. Assigning the right to payment rarely changes the buyer's duty or risk, so it is freely assignable (§ 2-210(2)-(3)).
True. That is the interpretive rule of § 2-210(4), unless the circumstances indicate otherwise.

Correct. This is the false statement. No delegation relieves the delegating party of any duty to perform or any liability for breach (§ 2-210(1)); only a novation, which the other party must agree to, releases it.
topic: 1 · Assignment & delegation (§ 2-210) — Delegator not discharged

q: Big Bird orders crab cakes described on the menu as "all lump meat, shell-free." A sharp fragment of crab shell cuts his mouth. He sues the restaurant for breach of the implied warranty of merchantability. Which statement is most accurate?
o: He loses under every test, because crab shell is natural to crab.
He wins under every test, because any injury from food proves it was unmerchantable.
Under the reasonable-expectation test he likely wins, because a diner reasonably expects "shell-free" crab cakes to have no shell.
He wins only if the restaurant was negligent in preparing the crab cakes.
He loses, because serving food in a restaurant is a service, not a sale of goods.
oe: That is only the foreign-natural test's result. The reasonable-expectation test focuses on what the diner could expect, especially given the menu.
Under the foreign-natural test, a natural substance doesn't make food unmerchantable.

Correct. The reasonable-expectation test asks what a reasonable consumer would expect, and the menu promised no shell. Under the older foreign-natural test, shell is natural to crab and the diner would likely lose.
Implied warranties impose strict liability; negligence isn't required.
Serving food or drink for value is a sale (§ 2-314(1)).
topic: 4 · Implied warranties (§§ 2-314, 2-315) — Food: two tests

q: A printing company buys a press under a contract making "repair or replacement of defective parts" the buyer's "sole and exclusive remedy." Over eight months, the seller tries six times to fix a recurring jam and never succeeds. What remedies does the buyer now have?
o: Only more repair attempts, because the buyer agreed repair was its exclusive remedy.
None, because the buyer accepted the press and so waived its remedies.
Only a refund of the price, because that is the default substitute remedy.
Only damages capped at the cost of a replacement part.
Its ordinary UCC remedies; the limited remedy has failed of its essential purpose.
oe: An exclusive remedy gives way when it fails of its essential purpose (§ 2-719(2)).
Acceptance doesn't waive remedies for breach (§ 2-607(2)), and the buyer may still be able to revoke acceptance (§ 2-608).
§ 2-719(2) restores the full range of Code remedies, not just a refund.
Once the limited remedy fails, its limits fall away.

Correct. When circumstances cause an exclusive or limited remedy to fail of its essential purpose, remedy may be had as provided in the UCC (§ 2-719(2)). Repeated unsuccessful repairs over a long period are the classic example.
topic: 8 · Limited remedies (§ 2-719) — Repeated failed repairs

q: Kermit contracts to sell 200 standard steel folding chairs to Sam Eagle's convention hall. The contract says nothing about delegation. Overbooked, Kermit arranges for Rowlf, another chair dealer, to deliver 200 identical chairs on the delivery date. Sam refuses them, saying he made his deal with Kermit, not Rowlf. Is Sam entitled to refuse?
o: No. Kermit may delegate, but he remains liable if Rowlf's chairs are nonconforming.
No, but only if Rowlf is a merchant who deals in chairs of that kind.
No, and once Rowlf tenders the chairs, Kermit is released from the contract.
Yes, because only a buyer, not a seller, may delegate contractual duties.
Yes, because a party may never delegate its duties without first obtaining the other party's consent.
oe: Correct. Absent a contrary agreement or a substantial interest in Kermit's own performance, Kermit may delegate (§ 2-210(1)). Identical standard chairs give Sam no such interest, and Kermit stays on the hook for any breach.
§ 2-210(1) doesn't ask whether the delegate is a merchant. It asks whether Sam has a substantial interest in having Kermit himself perform.
Sam must take the chairs, but delegation never releases the delegator from liability for breach (§ 2-210(1)).
Both buyers and sellers may delegate. In fact, sellers' duties are the ones most often delegated.
Consent isn't required. Delegation is the default rule for both buyers and sellers (§ 2-210(1)).
topic: 1 · Assignment & delegation (§ 2-210) — Delegating standard goods

q: Bunsen's Brewery orders a custom brewing system for its new taproom, scheduled to open May 1. After discussing projected sales, the two merchants negotiate a clause: "Seller shall pay $500 per day of late delivery as liquidated damages." The system arrives 20 days late. The seller proves that because of slow spring traffic, the brewery's actual lost profit was only $1,500. Can the brewery recover $10,000?
o: Only $1,500, because liquidated damages are always reduced to the buyer's proven loss.
Probably yes, because the amount was reasonable in light of the harm the parties anticipated when they contracted.
No, because the clause was not printed in conspicuous type.
No, because the clause yields more than six times the actual harm and is therefore a penalty.
Yes, because courts never review liquidated damages clauses negotiated between merchants.
oe: That would make liquidated damages pointless. A valid clause fixes the amount regardless of later-proven loss.

Correct. § 2-718(1) measures reasonableness against the anticipated or actual harm. A negotiated figure based on projected profits, where lost profits were hard to prove, is reasonable when made, even if actual harm turns out smaller.
Nothing in § 2-718 requires a liquidated damages clause to be conspicuous.
Actual harm can be considered, but the disjunctive "anticipated or actual" lets a court enforce a clause that was reasonable when made. The stronger view enforces it here.
Merchant status doesn't remove the § 2-718(1) reasonableness test. An unreasonably large amount is void as a penalty even between merchants.
topic: 2 · Liquidated damages (§ 2-718) — Anticipated vs. actual harm

q: Bert's contract to supply Ernie's restaurant with handmade pasta says: "Neither party may assign this contract." Bert later sends the restaurant pasta made by a different pasta maker under Bert's label. The pasta is equal in quality. Ernie objects. Who is right?
o: Ernie, but only because handmade pasta always gives the buyer a substantial interest in the original maker.
Bert, because the clause is unenforceable as a restraint on alienation.
Bert, because the substitute pasta is equal in quality and Ernie suffers no harm.
Ernie, because a ban on assigning "the contract" is generally read to bar delegation of performance.
Bert, because the clause bans only assignments of rights, and Bert assigned nothing.
oe: Ernie may well have such an interest, but he doesn't need it. The contract clause alone bars the delegation.
Restraints on assigning rights to payment are overridden by § 9-406(d), but parties may freely bar delegation of performance.
Equal quality would matter if the contract were silent. Here the parties agreed otherwise, and § 2-210(1) honors that agreement.

Correct. Under § 2-210(4), a prohibition on assigning "the contract" is construed (unless the circumstances indicate otherwise) as barring only the delegation of the assignor's performance. That is exactly what Bert did.
It's the reverse. § 2-210(4) reads "assign this contract" as a bar on delegating duties, not on assigning rights.
topic: 1 · Assignment & delegation (§ 2-210) — "Assign this contract" ban: delegation

q: A contract for a $200,000 custom packaging line, drafted by the seller, says: "Liquidated damages for Seller's failure to deliver shall be $10." The seller never delivers, and the buyer suffers large provable losses. Which statement is most accurate?
o: The clause must be enforced, because § 2-718 limits only clauses that are too large.
The buyer may recover only $10 unless the clause was conspicuous.
The clause is void as a penalty, because it is unreasonable in light of the anticipated harm.
It isn't a penalty, but a court may strike it as unconscionable.
The clause is automatically valid because the buyer could have negotiated a larger amount.
oe: The penalty rule addresses large amounts, but unconscionability can still reach an absurdly small one.
Conspicuousness isn't the test. A conspicuous $10 clause could still be struck as unconscionable.
"Penalty" describes an unreasonably large amount that punishes the breaching party. A $10 figure punishes no one.
Correct. § 2-718(1) voids only unreasonably large amounts as penalties. Comment 1 notes that an unreasonably small amount might be stricken under the unconscionability section (§ 2-302).
Opportunity to bargain is relevant to unconscionability but doesn't make the term automatically valid.
topic: 2 · Liquidated damages (§ 2-718) — Unreasonably small amount

q: Miss Piggy signs a contract to buy a dining table described in the contract as "solid walnut." A later paragraph states: "Seller makes no warranties, express or implied." The table is walnut veneer over particleboard. Can Miss Piggy recover for breach of express warranty?
o: Yes, but only if the disclaimer was not conspicuous.
No, because the contract expressly disclaims all warranties, express as well as implied.
No, because "solid walnut" is mere puffing.
No, because the parol evidence rule bars evidence of the description.
Yes; the general disclaimer can't negate the contract's own description.
oe: Conspicuousness doesn't save a disclaimer of an express warranty that's part of the bargain.
§ 2-316(1) makes the disclaimer inoperative to the extent it conflicts with the description.
"Solid walnut" is a specific, verifiable description of the goods.
The description is in the signed writing itself, so the parol evidence rule doesn't touch it.

Correct. Words creating an express warranty and words negating it are read consistently where reasonable; otherwise the negation is inoperative (§ 2-316(1)). A general disclaimer can't cut down the contract's own description (§ 2-313 cmt. 4).
topic: 6 · Warranty disclaimers (§ 2-316) — Express description vs. disclaimer

q: Pepe sells Rizzo a guitar for $40,000 under a signed bill of sale warranting that it is "an original 1959 model." Before closing, Rizzo's own appraiser tells him the serial number looks suspicious. Pepe himself says nothing about any doubts. Rizzo buys anyway, and the guitar proves to be a 1980s reissue. Can Rizzo recover for breach of express warranty?
o: No, because Rizzo had to reserve his rights in writing before closing, whatever the source of his doubts.
Yes, but only if Rizzo proves he relied on the warranty and not on his appraiser.
No, because Rizzo is more expert than Pepe, so the statement is mere opinion.
No, because a buyer who suspects a warranted fact is false can't treat it as part of the basis of the bargain.
Probably yes, because doubts he learned from his own appraiser don't defeat the warranty; he may have bought it as insurance.
oe: Reservation of rights matters only when the seller is the one who disclosed the facts that breach the warranty.
Comment 3 to § 2-313 says no particular reliance need be shown. The seller must offer clear affirmative proof to remove an affirmation from the bargain.
A dated, verifiable attribution in a signed bill of sale is an affirmation of fact, whoever is more expert.
That overstates the basis-of-the-bargain requirement. Doubts from a third party don't take the warranty out of the deal.

Correct. What matters is whether the buyer bought the seller's promise, not whether he believed the fact. A buyer who learns of doubts from a third party may still rely on the warranty. Only knowledge disclosed by the seller itself, followed by closing without reserving rights, waives the breach.
topic: 3 · Express warranties (§ 2-313) — Buyer's doubts from own expert

q: Grover's Mill has a three-year contract to supply "all the flour required by Cookie Monster's Bakery," a single shop. Cookie assigns his rights under the contract to Mega Bakes Corp., which runs 40 bakeries and plans to fill all of their flour needs under it. Grover objects. Is the assignment effective?
o: Yes, as long as Mega Bakes's requirements are ordered in good faith.
Yes, because the contract doesn't prohibit assignment.
No, because a requirements contract lacks mutuality and so is unenforceable by any assignee.
Yes, because a buyer's right to receive goods is always freely assignable.
No, because it would materially change Grover's duty and materially increase his burden.
oe: Good faith governs quantity under § 2-306, but it doesn't cure an assignment that materially changes the seller's duty.
Silence removes only the contract limit. The statutory limit on material changes in the other party's duty still applies.
Requirements contracts are enforceable (§ 2-306). The problem is the change in Grover's duty, not mutuality.
It is assignable only within the § 2-210(2) limits, which this assignment exceeds.

Correct. Rights can't be assigned when the assignment would materially change the other party's duty or materially increase its burden or risk (§ 2-210(2)). Swapping one shop's requirements for 40 bakeries' requirements does both (see § 2-210 cmt. 4).
topic: 1 · Assignment & delegation (§ 2-210) — Requirements contract assigned

q: Waldorf contracts to buy a used printing press from Statler's Supply for $30,000. Before delivery, Waldorf assigns "all my rights under the contract" to Pepe, who accepts. Statler delivers the press to Pepe, who never pays. From whom may Statler recover the price?
o: Only from Pepe, because Waldorf transferred his duty to pay along with his rights.
From either Pepe or Waldorf, though Statler may collect only once.
From neither, because an assignment of rights transfers no duties to the assignee.
Only from Pepe, and only if Statler consented to the assignment in advance.
Only from Waldorf, because Statler never made a contract with Pepe.
oe: Delegation never relieves the delegating party of liability (§ 2-210(1)). Waldorf is still on the hook.

Correct. A general assignment of "all my rights" is also a delegation of the assignor's duties, and the assignee's acceptance is a promise to perform that the other original party can enforce (§ 2-210(5)). Waldorf, the delegator, remains liable too (§ 2-210(1)).
An assignment of "all my rights" is presumptively a delegation as well (§ 2-210(5)).
Statler's consent isn't needed for the assignment, and Waldorf remains liable either way.
Statler doesn't need a contract with Pepe. § 2-210(5) makes Pepe's acceptance a promise to perform that Statler may enforce.
topic: 1 · Assignment & delegation (§ 2-210) — "All my rights" accepted

q: A candy maker buys an industrial mixer under a negotiated contract with two separate clauses: (1) an exclusive repair-or-replace remedy, and (2) a conspicuous exclusion of all consequential damages. The repair remedy fails of its essential purpose, and the candy maker sues for $90,000 in lost profits. The state follows the majority (independent) approach. What is the most likely result?
o: It may recover the lost profits only if the exclusion was not conspicuous.
It may recover direct damages, but the exclusion of lost profits stands unless that clause is itself unconscionable.
It may recover the lost profits, because when the repair remedy fails, every limit on remedies falls with it.
It may recover the lost profits, because excluding consequential damages is prima facie unconscionable.
It may recover nothing, because its exclusive remedy was repair or replacement.
oe: § 2-719 has no conspicuousness requirement. The test is unconscionability.

Correct. Under the independent approach, the consequential-damages exclusion is judged on its own under § 2-719(3) and survives the failure of the repair remedy unless unconscionable. Excluding commercial lost profits in a negotiated deal is not.
That is the minority (dependent) approach. The majority tests the exclusion separately.
That presumption applies only to personal injury from consumer goods. Limiting commercial loss is not prima facie unconscionable.
The failed limited remedy gives way under § 2-719(2), so direct damages are available.
topic: 8 · Limited remedies (§ 2-719) — Independent approach: commercial loss

q: A quarry tells a pump dealer it needs a pump that can drain its pit at 80 gallons per minute and relies on the dealer to choose one. The dealer's invoice expressly warrants that the pump it selects is "rated at 50 gallons per minute." The pump delivers exactly 50 gallons per minute. The dealer argues its express warranty displaces any implied warranty. Who wins?
o: The dealer, because express warranties always displace inconsistent implied warranties.
The dealer, because the quarry should have supplied its own technical specifications.
The quarry, because express warranties don't displace the fitness warranty.
The quarry, but only under the implied warranty of merchantability.
The dealer, because the pump met its express rating, so there was no breach.
oe: § 2-317(c) makes an exception for the implied warranty of fitness.
Buyer-supplied specs would defeat reliance, but here the quarry relied on the dealer's selection.

Correct. Warranties are cumulative; when they can't be reconciled, express warranties displace inconsistent implied warranties other than fitness for a particular purpose (§ 2-317(c)). The quarry's fitness claim survives.
A 50-gpm pump that pumps 50 gpm is likely fit for its ordinary purpose; the quarry's claim is fitness.
Meeting the express rating doesn't satisfy the separate fitness warranty for the quarry's 80-gallon need.
topic: 7 · Privity & cumulation (§§ 2-317, 2-318) — Express vs. fitness: cumulation

q: Elmo agrees to buy a $10,000 used piano from Hooper's Music and pays a $3,000 deposit. The contract has no liquidated damages term. Elmo repudiates, and Hooper's justifiably withholds delivery. Hooper's promptly resells the piano for $10,000 and proves no damages. How much of the deposit must Hooper's return?
oe: The seller may keep the smaller of 20% or $500 even without proving damages (§ 2-718(2)(b)).
Forfeiture of the whole deposit requires a valid liquidated damages term or provable damages; Hooper's has neither.

Correct. With no liquidated damages term, the seller may keep 20% of the value of the buyer's total performance or $500, whichever is smaller (§ 2-718(2)(b)). The smaller is $500, and Hooper's proved no damages to offset, so it returns $3,000 - $500 = $2,500.
That keeps 20% ($2,000). § 2-718(2)(b) uses the smaller of 20% or $500.
That figure confuses the 20% amount with the refund. The refund is the deposit less $500.
topic: 2 · Liquidated damages (§ 2-718) — Deposit: no LD term

q: Rosita's Flower Shop sells its five-year-old delivery van to Telly for $9,000. The shop has never sold a vehicle before. A week later, the van's transmission fails. Did the shop give Telly an implied warranty of merchantability?
o: Yes, because the van failed within a week.
Yes, because any business that sells goods is a merchant for all purposes.
No, because this is not an Article 2 transaction.
No, because the shop is not a merchant with respect to vans.
No, because implied warranties never apply to used goods.
oe: Early failure may prove breach, but only if a warranty arose in the first place.
Merchant status for § 2-314 is goods-specific. Being in business generally isn't enough.
A sale of a van is a sale of goods, squarely within Article 2.
Correct. Merchantability is implied only if the seller is a merchant with respect to goods of that kind (§ 2-314(1)). A florist selling its own van in an isolated sale isn't one (cmt. 3).
They can, with a reduced content. The problem here is that the seller isn't a merchant in vans.
topic: 4 · Implied warranties (§§ 2-314, 2-315) — Not a merchant in goods of the kind

q: Julia buys a new SUV from a dealer. The manufacturer's warranty, which limits her remedy to repair and states in bold capitals that consequential damages are excluded, is printed only in the owner's manual in the glove box. Nothing in the sale documents mentions it, and she never sees it until weeks later. Repairs fail repeatedly. In a state following the independent approach, is the consequential-damages exclusion enforceable?
o: Yes, because it was printed in bold capitals.
Probably not, because a limitation the buyer couldn't see until after contracting is procedurally unconscionable however clear its type.
Yes, because under the independent approach the exclusion survives the failure of the repair remedy.
Yes, because Julia could have asked to read the warranty before buying.
No, because consequential-damages exclusions are never enforceable in consumer sales.
oe: Clear type doesn't help when the buyer had no chance to see the term before contracting.

Correct. Even under the independent approach, the exclusion falls if it's unconscionable (§ 2-719(3)). A limitation available to the buyer only after she made the contract is unconscionable however conspicuous it is.
It survives the failure only if it isn't unconscionable, and this one likely is.
Nothing showed the warranty was available to her before signing, and that's the decisive fact.
They're enforceable unless unconscionable; only personal-injury exclusions in consumer goods are prima facie unconscionable.
topic: 8 · Limited remedies (§ 2-719) — Exclusion seen only after sale

q: Linda buys a hair dryer for home use. The manufacturer's warranty excludes "all consequential damages of any kind." The dryer overheats and burns Linda's hand. Which statement is most accurate?
o: The exclusion is valid, because consequential damages may always be excluded.
The exclusion is valid, because personal injury is governed only by tort law.
The exclusion is prima facie unconscionable as applied to Linda's personal injury.
The exclusion is conclusively void, and the seller can't offer any evidence to save it.
The exclusion is void only if it was not conspicuous.
oe: Exclusions are allowed unless unconscionable, and § 2-719(3) presumes this one is.
Personal injury proximately caused by a breach of warranty is consequential damage under § 2-715(2)(b).

Correct. Limiting consequential damages for injury to the person in the case of consumer goods is prima facie unconscionable (§ 2-719(3)). The seller may try to rebut the presumption, but it starts against the seller.
"Prima facie" means a rebuttable presumption, not a conclusive rule.
Conspicuousness isn't the test; unconscionability is.
topic: 8 · Limited remedies (§ 2-719) — Consumer personal injury

q: A commercial bakery orders a $40,000 dough sheeter by phone after the dealer recommends that model for its volume. When the machine is delivered, the bakery's manager signs a delivery receipt. On the back, in large capitals, it says: "SELLER DISCLAIMS ALL IMPLIED WARRANTIES, INCLUDING MERCHANTABILITY." The machine can't keep up with the bakery's volume. Is the disclaimer effective?
o: Probably not, because the contract was formed before delivery, and the receipt's disclaimer never became part of it.
No, because a disclaimer must appear on the front of a document to be effective.
Yes, because the disclaimer mentions merchantability and is in large capitals.
Yes, because the manager signed the receipt.
Yes, but it excludes only the implied warranty of fitness.
oe: Correct. Before applying § 2-316, ask whether the disclaimer is part of the contract. A disclaimer first appearing after formation is at most a proposed modification or an additional term that materially alters the deal (§ 2-207 cmt. 4). Signing a delivery receipt isn't assent to it.
Placement goes to conspicuousness. The deeper problem is that the term came after formation.
Form compliance doesn't matter if the term never became part of the contract.
Signing a delivery receipt acknowledges delivery; it doesn't show agreement to give up warranties.
If it were part of the contract it would reach both warranties; the problem is that it isn't.
topic: 6 · Warranty disclaimers (§ 2-316) — Disclaimer after the deal

q: After a tenant stops paying rent, a self-storage company holds a lien sale and auctions off the contents of the tenant's unit. Ernie buys a television from the unit. It later turns out the tenant had borrowed it from a friend, who reclaims it. Ernie sues the storage company for breach of the warranty of title. What is the most likely result?
o: Ernie wins, because the storage company is a merchant.
The storage company wins, because auctions never carry a warranty of title.
Ernie wins, because the title warranty can be excluded only by specific written language.
The storage company wins, because the circumstances gave Ernie reason to know it was selling only whatever rights the tenant had.
Ernie wins, because the borrower's friend has only a colorable claim.
oe: Merchant status doesn't matter to the title warranty; every seller makes it unless excluded.
An ordinary auctioneer's sale can carry a title warranty. It's the lien-sale circumstances that exclude it here.
§ 2-312(2) allows exclusion by specific language or by circumstances.

Correct. Title is excluded by circumstances that give the buyer reason to know the seller doesn't claim title itself (§ 2-312(2)). A lien sale of a defaulting tenant's goods is that kind of out-of-the-ordinary sale (cmt. 5).
The friend's claim is valid, not merely colorable, and in any event the warranty was excluded.
topic: 5 · Warranty of title & infringement (§ 2-312) — Title excluded by circumstances

q: A contract says: "Buyer may not assign any rights under this agreement, and any attempted assignment is void." The seller never delivers any of the goods. The buyer assigns its claim for damages for the seller's total breach to a collection firm. Is the assignment effective?
o: Yes, because anti-assignment clauses are never enforceable under Article 2.
Yes, because a claim for damages for breach of the whole contract is assignable despite the ban.
No, because the contract expressly states that any attempted assignment by the buyer is void.
Yes, but only if the seller consents after the breach occurs.
No, because only a seller's right to payment for goods can be assigned in the face of a contractual ban.
oe: They can be. A valid prohibition can make an assignment of other rights ineffective; this claim is simply an exception.
Correct. § 2-210(2) expressly allows assignment of a right to damages for breach of the whole contract, notwithstanding a contrary agreement.
The "void" language can't block this particular right. § 2-210(2) carves out claims for breach of the whole contract.
The statute makes the assignment effective without the breaching seller's consent.
§ 9-406(d) protects rights to payment, but § 2-210(2) separately protects a claim for damages for breach of the whole contract.
topic: 1 · Assignment & delegation (§ 2-210) — Damages claim despite ban

q: Gonzo's Cannon Works contracts to build and deliver 50 circus cannons to Camilla's circus over the next year. Gonzo then assigns the contract to Rizzo Rat Works, a startup Camilla has never heard of, which accepts. Camilla is worried Rizzo can't do the job. What may Camilla do?
o: Demand adequate assurance from Rizzo.
Nothing, because she has no right to object to a permitted delegation.
Cancel the contract at once, because the delegation is an anticipatory repudiation.
Sue Gonzo immediately for damages, because a delegation is itself a breach.
Demand assurance only from Gonzo, because Rizzo owes Camilla nothing.
oe: Correct. Under § 2-210(6), the other party may treat an assignment that delegates performance as creating reasonable grounds for insecurity and may demand assurances from the assignee, without prejudice to its rights against the assignor.
Even a permitted delegation gives the other party grounds for insecurity under § 2-210(6).
Delegating isn't repudiating. Camilla's remedy is to demand assurance, then treat a failure to give it as a repudiation (§ 2-609(4)).
Absent a contractual ban or a substantial interest, delegation is permitted and isn't a breach.
Rizzo accepted an assignment of the contract, so it promised to perform (§ 2-210(5)), and § 2-210(6) lets Camilla demand assurance from the assignee.
topic: 1 · Assignment & delegation (§ 2-210) — Delegation and assurance

q: Abby contracts to buy a custom storefront sign for $12,000 and prepays $4,000. The contract validly liquidates the seller's damages for Abby's breach at $1,000. Abby repudiates, and the sign maker justifiably stops work and withholds delivery. Abby has received no benefit from the contract. How much is Abby entitled to get back?
oe: A valid liquidated damages term lets the seller keep the liquidated amount out of the prepayment.
That keeps 20% of the price ($2,400). The 20% figure belongs to the default rule, which a valid liquidated damages term displaces.

Correct. When the seller justifiably withholds delivery because of the buyer's breach, the buyer gets restitution of the amount by which its payments exceed the valid liquidated amount (§ 2-718(2)(a)): $4,000 - $1,000 = $3,000.
The smaller-of-20%-or-$500 rule applies only when there is no liquidated damages term (§ 2-718(2)(b)).
Keeping the whole $4,000 would exceed the agreed liquidated amount, a forfeiture § 2-718(2) forbids.
topic: 2 · Liquidated damages (§ 2-718) — Prepayment over the LD amount

q: Which statement best describes how a warranty disclaimer differs from a remedy limitation?
o: A disclaimer means no breach; a limitation restricts recovery after a breach.
They are the same thing, and both are governed by § 2-316.
A disclaimer applies only to express warranties; a limitation applies only to implied warranties.
A disclaimer must be conspicuous; a limitation must be signed separately by the buyer.
A disclaimer limits consequential damages; a limitation eliminates the warranty entirely.
oe: Correct. A disclaimer attacks the contract/breach element by removing the warranty. A limitation attacks the damages element by restricting the remedy for a breach that did occur (§§ 2-316(4), 2-719).
§ 2-316 governs disclaimers; §§ 2-718 and 2-719 govern limitations.
Disclaimers mostly concern implied warranties, and limitations can restrict remedies for breach of any warranty.
The first half is partly true for some disclaimers, but no rule requires separate signing of a limitation.
That reverses the two concepts.
topic: 8 · Limited remedies (§ 2-719) — Disclaimer vs. limitation

q: In each contract below, the agreement says nothing about assignment or delegation. Which transfer is most likely ineffective?
o: A bridal designer, chosen for her signature style, hands the design and sewing of a custom gown to another shop.
A buyer of 1,000 standard pallets, F.O.B. seller's plant, assigns its right to receive them to an affiliate that will pick them up.
A seller of bagged road salt has a warehouse company load and deliver the salt.
A buyer has its parent company pay the price on the due date.
A lumber seller assigns its right to the buyer's payment to its bank.
oe: Correct. A buyer of specially made goods chosen for the maker's personal style has a substantial interest in having that maker perform, so the designer can't delegate (§ 2-210(1)).
Pickup at the seller's plant by a different company doesn't materially change the seller's duty or risk (§ 2-210(2)).
Delivering fungible goods is a classic permitted delegation. The buyer has no stake in who loads the truck.
Payment is payment. The seller has no substantial interest in which entity writes the check, and the buyer remains liable.
Assigning a right to payment almost never materially changes the buyer's duty, so it's effective (§ 2-210(2)-(3)).
topic: 1 · Assignment & delegation (§ 2-210) — Which transfer fails

q: A merchant seller's signed contract states, in bold capitals just above the signature line: "THERE ARE NO WARRANTIES, EXPRESS OR IMPLIED, WITH THIS SALE." Measured against the requirements of § 2-316(2), which implied warranties does this language exclude?
o: Both merchantability and fitness.
Neither, because the clause doesn't mention either warranty by name.
Fitness for a particular purpose only.
Merchantability only.
Merchantability, fitness, and the warranty of title.
oe: The clause works for fitness but not merchantability under § 2-316(2), because it never mentions merchantability.
Fitness doesn't have to be named; a conspicuous writing is enough.

Correct. Fitness may be excluded by any conspicuous writing (§ 2-316(2)). Merchantability requires language that mentions "merchantability," which this clause doesn't. (Some courts accept general language under § 2-316(3)(a), but § 2-316(2) alone doesn't.)
Merchantability can't be excluded under § 2-316(2) without mentioning it.
Title is excluded only by specific language or circumstances (§ 2-312(2)), and the clause fails for merchantability anyway.
topic: 6 · Warranty disclaimers (§ 2-316) — General disclaimer vs. § 2-316(2)

q: Oscar tells a camping-store clerk he needs a sleeping bag for winter camping at -20°F. The clerk recommends a bag rated to -30°F. Oscar says, "No, I only buy Grouch-Pro," and buys a Grouch-Pro bag rated to 20°F. He nearly freezes on his trip. Does Oscar have a claim for breach of the implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose?
o: Yes, but only if the fitness warranty was stated in writing.
Yes, because the store is a merchant that sells sleeping bags.
No, because winter camping is an ordinary purpose for a sleeping bag.
No, because Oscar didn't rely on the seller's skill or judgment.
Yes, because the clerk knew Oscar's particular purpose.
oe: Implied warranties arise by law; they're never written.
Merchant status matters for § 2-314, not § 2-315. A merchant still makes no fitness warranty without reliance.
Use at -20°F is a particular purpose. The claim fails for lack of reliance, not because the purpose was ordinary.
Correct. Fitness requires actual reliance on the seller's skill or judgment (§ 2-315). A buyer who insists on a particular brand over the seller's recommendation isn't relying on the seller (cmt. 5).
Reason to know the purpose is only half the test. The seller must also have reason to know of reliance, and the buyer must actually rely.
topic: 4 · Implied warranties (§§ 2-314, 2-315) — Fitness: brand insistence

q: A contract for a commercial walk-in freezer makes "replacement with an identical unit" the buyer's exclusive remedy. The freezer fails in month two. The manufacturer has discontinued the model, and no identical unit exists anywhere. What is the most likely result?
o: The buyer gets nothing, because it agreed to an exclusive remedy that can no longer be performed.
The seller may substitute any freezer of its choosing, of whatever quality.
The contract is discharged for impracticability, so neither party owes anything.
The remedy fails of its essential purpose, so ordinary UCC remedies apply.
The buyer may recover only the price of a replacement part.
oe: That leaves the buyer with no remedy at all. § 2-719(2) prevents exactly that.
The seller can't rewrite the agreed remedy. With replacement impossible, the Code's remedies apply.
The seller's inability to perform the agreed remedy doesn't excuse its breach of warranty.
Correct. An exclusive remedy that can't be performed deprives the buyer of the substantial value of the bargain and fails of its essential purpose (§ 2-719(2), cmt. 1).
The contract promised a whole unit, and in any event the failed limit falls away.
topic: 8 · Limited remedies (§ 2-719) — Replacement impossible

q: Before ordering 50 bags of coffee beans described in the contract as "Colombian Supremo," Zoe's café is given a sample bag drawn from the seller's warehouse lot and agrees to buy "beans like the sample." The delivered beans are genuine Colombian Supremo but a noticeably lower grade than the sample. Is the seller in breach?
o: No, because a sample creates a warranty only if the seller calls it a "guarantee."
No, because Zoe could have tested the delivered beans before accepting them.
Yes, but only if the seller is a merchant with respect to coffee.
Yes, because the sample was part of the bargain, so the whole lot must conform to it.
No, because the beans match the written contract description, which controls over any sample.
oe: No formal words are needed (§ 2-313(2)).
A chance to inspect doesn't eliminate an express warranty; Zoe may still sue for breach after acceptance.
Express warranties, including those by sample, can be made by any seller.

Correct. A sample made part of the bargain warrants that the whole of the goods will conform (§ 2-313(1)(c)). A sample drawn from an existing bulk also displaces inconsistent general words of description (§ 2-317(b)).
When a sample from an existing bulk and a general description conflict, the sample generally controls (§ 2-317(b)).
topic: 3 · Express warranties (§ 2-313) — Sample from the bulk

q: Count von Count buys a new dishwasher from a local retailer, which bought it from a distributor, which bought it from the manufacturer. It never cleans properly. The retailer has gone out of business, so the Count sues the manufacturer for economic loss under the implied warranty of merchantability. The state's courts have abolished the vertical-privity requirement for such claims. What is the most likely result?
o: The Count loses, because § 2-318 never extends warranties to economic loss.
The Count may proceed only on an express warranty, because implied warranties never run past the immediate seller.
The Count loses, because only the retailer made him an implied warranty.
The Count may proceed only if he was injured in person.
The Count may proceed against the manufacturer even though he bought from an intermediary.
oe: § 2-318 addresses horizontal reach; it leaves vertical privity to the courts (cmt. 3), and these courts have abolished it.
Once vertical privity is abolished, implied warranties can run past the immediate seller.
Without a vertical-privity requirement, the manufacturer's implied warranty can run to the remote buyer.
The abolition here covers economic loss. Personal injury is a § 2-318 horizontal-privity question.

Correct. Where vertical privity is abolished, a consumer may sue the remote manufacturer for economic loss on the implied warranty of merchantability even though the consumer bought from someone else in the distribution chain.
topic: 7 · Privity & cumulation (§§ 2-317, 2-318) — Remote manufacturer

q: To secure a business loan, Rosita's Rugs assigns to Sesame Bank "all of Rosita's rights under" her contract to sell 300 rugs to a hotel. Rosita then fails to deliver the rugs. The hotel sues Sesame Bank for breach. What is the most likely result?
o: The hotel wins, because an assignment of "all rights" always includes a delegation of duties.
The bank wins, because a hotel cannot sue anyone except the original seller in any case.
The hotel wins, because the bank holds the right to the price and must therefore deliver the goods.
The hotel wins, but only if the bank received notice of the hotel's claim before the loan.
The bank wins, because an assignment for security doesn't delegate the assignor's duties.
oe: Not always. § 2-210(5) names an assignment for security as the standard example of circumstances showing no delegation.
An assignee who accepts a delegation can be sued by the other party (§ 2-210(5)). The bank wins only because there was no delegation.
Holding the right to payment as collateral doesn't make the bank a delegate. Rosita alone owes the rugs.
Notice doesn't turn a security assignment into a promise to perform.

Correct. § 2-210(5) treats a general assignment of rights as a delegation of duties unless the language or the circumstances, as in an assignment for security, indicate otherwise. The bank never promised to deliver rugs.
topic: 1 · Assignment & delegation (§ 2-210) — Assignment for security

q: Gonzo orders 5,000 T-shirts from a print shop and supplies the logo artwork himself. A company sues the print shop, claiming the logo infringes its trademark. Which statement is most accurate?
o: The print shop wins only if it is not a merchant regularly dealing in T-shirts.
Gonzo must hold the print shop harmless, because he supplied the design.
The print shop must indemnify Gonzo, because a merchant warrants goods free of infringement claims.
No one bears the risk until a court finds the trademark claim valid.
The print shop bears the risk, because it should have checked trademark registrations.
oe: Merchant status determines whether the seller gives an infringement warranty, but the buyer's hold-harmless duty applies either way.
Correct. A buyer who furnishes specifications must hold the seller harmless against infringement claims arising out of compliance with them (§ 2-312(3)).
The merchant's infringement warranty doesn't cover claims caused by the buyer's own specifications.
Under § 2-312(3) the duty to hold harmless arises from the claim; final proof of infringement isn't required first.
The statute places the risk on the buyer who supplied the design.
topic: 5 · Warranty of title & infringement (§ 2-312) — Infringement: buyer's design

q: A contract for 2,000 custom display cases says: "For each full week of delay, Seller shall pay Buyer 2% of the contract price, up to a maximum of 10%." The clause appears in ordinary type in the middle of a long paragraph. The seller argues the clause is unenforceable (1) because it states a formula rather than a dollar amount, and (2) because it isn't conspicuous. Which argument is correct?
o: Argument (1) only.
Argument (2) only.
Both (1) and (2).
Both, but only if the seller is a merchant.
None of the above.
oe: A liquidated damages clause may specify an amount or a formula for calculating damages.
Unlike a warranty disclaimer, a liquidated damages clause need not be conspicuous.
Neither argument is correct.
Merchant status doesn't matter. Formulas are permitted, and no conspicuousness rule applies to liquidated damages.

Correct. Neither argument works. A liquidated damages clause may use a formula, and § 2-718 has no conspicuousness requirement. The only question is whether the formula is reasonable under § 2-718(1).
topic: 2 · Liquidated damages (§ 2-718) — Formula; not conspicuous

q: A contract for a commercial ice machine says: "Seller's liability for late delivery shall not exceed $5,000." The machine arrives 10 days late, and the buyer proves $1,200 in actual damages from the delay. How much can the buyer recover?
o: Nothing, because a cap is unenforceable unless it is conspicuous.
$5,000, unless the seller proves the buyer's actual loss was smaller.
$2,500, half the cap, as a reasonable estimate of delay damages.
oe: Correct. "Shall not exceed" language is a cap, a limitation of remedy under § 2-719, not liquidated damages. The buyer must prove actual damages and recovers them up to the cap.
Remedy limitations, like liquidated damages clauses, need not be conspicuous.
The buyer would recover $5,000 only if the clause fixed damages at that sum. A cap sets a ceiling, not an amount.
That treats the cap as liquidated damages with a rebuttal. A cap never awards more than proven loss.
Nothing supports splitting the cap. The buyer recovers what it proves, up to $5,000.
topic: 2 · Liquidated damages (§ 2-718) — Cap vs. liquidated damages

q: A distributor's contract for 50 commercial dishwashers limits the buyer's remedy to refund of the price. The limitation is printed in the same type as the rest of the contract, in paragraph 14 of 20. The buyer argues the limitation is unenforceable because it is not conspicuous. Is the buyer right?
o: Yes, because every term that reduces a buyer's rights must be conspicuous.
No, because § 2-719 doesn't require a remedy limitation to be conspicuous.
Yes, unless the buyer actually read paragraph 14.
Yes, because § 2-316's conspicuousness rule governs remedy limitations too.
No, but only because both parties are merchants.
oe: No such general rule exists. Conspicuousness is required for certain § 2-316 disclaimers only.
Correct. Unlike disclaimers of merchantability (in writing) and fitness, remedy limitations need not be conspicuous. They are tested by failure of essential purpose and unconscionability.
Whether the buyer read it doesn't matter to enforceability under § 2-719.
§ 2-316(4) sends remedy limitations to §§ 2-718 and 2-719, which have no such rule.
The answer is the same for consumers; § 2-719 has no conspicuousness requirement for anyone.
topic: 8 · Limited remedies (§ 2-719) — Conspicuousness not required

q: Snuffy, who has never sold tires before, sells his old snow tires to his neighbor Herry, saying, "These have less than 5,000 miles on them." In fact they have 40,000 miles and are badly worn. Herry sues for breach of warranty. What is the most likely result?
o: Snuffy wins, because only merchants make warranties under Article 2.
Herry wins on the implied warranty of merchantability.
Herry wins, because any seller can make an express warranty.
Snuffy wins, because his statement was oral and the price was low.
Snuffy wins, because the tires were sold used.
oe: Only the merchantability warranty requires a merchant. Express warranties and the title warranty don't.
Snuffy isn't a merchant with respect to tires, so no merchantability warranty arose.
Correct. A specific mileage figure is an affirmation of fact (§ 2-313(1)(a)). Express warranties don't require a merchant seller; only the implied warranty of merchantability does (§ 2-314).
Oral statements count, and a low price doesn't turn a specific fact into opinion.
Used goods can carry express warranties.
topic: 3 · Express warranties (§ 2-313) — Casual seller's express warranty

q: Animal's Drum Co. sells $10,000 of drum kits to a music school and assigns the right to payment to a factor, which notifies the school. The school accepts the kits, then discovers hidden defects that give it a $2,000 warranty claim against Animal's. The factor demands $10,000. How much must the school pay the factor?
o: $8,000, because the school may assert its warranty claim against the factor.
$10,000, because the school must pay the assignee in full and then sue Animal's.
$10,000, because the school's acceptance waived all warranty claims.
Nothing until Animal's repairs the drums, because the assignment suspended the school's duty to pay.
Nothing, because the goods were nonconforming when tendered.
oe: Correct. An assignee steps into the assignor's shoes and takes subject to the account debtor's defenses and claims arising from the contract (see § 9-404). The school may reduce what it pays the factor by its $2,000 warranty claim.
The assignee gets no better rights than the assignor had. The school can raise its warranty claim against the factor.
Acceptance doesn't waive warranty claims as long as the buyer gives timely notice of breach (§ 2-607(3)(a)).
The assignment didn't suspend anything. The school's duty runs to the factor, reduced by its defenses.
The school accepted the kits, so it owes the price less its damages from the nonconformity (§§ 2-607(1), 2-714).
topic: 1 · Assignment & delegation (§ 2-210) — Assignee subject to defenses

q: Two merchants agree that if the seller fails to deliver a custom kiln, the seller "shall pay $5,000 as liquidated damages." The amount was a reasonable estimate when made. The seller never delivers, and the buyer's actual losses turn out to be $20,000. What can the buyer most likely recover?
o: $20,000, because a clause that undercompensates is void as a penalty.
$25,000, the liquidated amount plus the actual loss.
$20,000, because a liquidated damages clause sets only a minimum recovery.
Nothing, because the buyer must elect between liquidated and actual damages before suing.
$5,000, because a valid clause fixes damages whether actual loss is higher or lower.
oe: A penalty is an unreasonably large amount. A reasonable estimate that turns out low isn't a penalty.
Liquidated damages replace actual damages for the covered breach; they aren't added to them.
A liquidated damages clause fixes the amount; it isn't a floor.
No election requirement exists. The valid clause measures the buyer's damages.
Correct. Liquidation is a two-way bargain. A reasonable liquidated amount replaces proof of actual damages, so the buyer is held to it even when actual loss turns out larger.
topic: 2 · Liquidated damages (§ 2-718) — Actual loss exceeds LD

q: A merchant buyer's contract for laboratory freezers provides: "Seller's total liability for any claim shall not exceed the price paid for the goods." Which statement is most accurate?
o: The cap is valid only if it is conspicuous.
The cap is a liquidated damages clause and must be reasonable in light of the anticipated harm.
The cap is a limitation of remedy, enforceable unless it fails of its essential purpose or is unconscionable.
Caps on damages are void in contracts for the sale of goods.
None of the above.
oe: Remedy limitations need not be conspicuous.
A cap is a limitation of remedy, not liquidated damages. It doesn't fix an amount; it sets a ceiling on proven damages.
Correct. § 2-719(1)(a) lets the parties limit or alter the measure of damages, subject to failure of essential purpose (§ 2-719(2)) and unconscionability (§ 2-302, § 2-719(3)).
§ 2-719(1)(a) expressly permits limiting the measure of damages.
C correctly states the rule.
topic: 8 · Limited remedies (§ 2-719) — Cap at the price

q: A fabricator orders 3,000 steel bolts from a distributor. Its purchase order refers to the distributor's spec sheet, which lists a tensile strength of 150,000 psi. The bolts test at 110,000 psi. The distributor argues it never "warranted" anything and the spec sheet was just technical data. Who wins?
o: The distributor, because technical data is opinion rather than fact.
The fabricator, but only under the implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose.
The fabricator, because the spec sheet's figures are a description of the goods that formed part of the bargain.
The distributor, because it never used the words "warrant" or "guarantee."
The distributor, because the fabricator should have tested the bolts before ordering.
oe: A stated tensile strength is specific, measurable, and verifiable: classic fact.
The better claim is express warranty. Nothing shows the fabricator relied on the distributor's skill to select the bolts.

Correct. Any description made part of the basis of the bargain creates an express warranty (§ 2-313(1)(b)). Technical specifications are descriptions (cmt. 5), and formal words like "warrant" aren't needed (§ 2-313(2)).
§ 2-313(2) says no formal words or specific intent to warrant are required.
Express warranties don't depend on the buyer's testing. Pre-contract examination affects implied warranties (§ 2-316(3)(b)).
topic: 3 · Express warranties (§ 2-313) — Spec sheet as description

q: Which of the following statements about the implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose is NOT correct?
o: The buyer must actually rely on the seller's skill or judgment.
The seller must have reason to know of the particular purpose at the time of contracting.
It arises only if the seller makes an affirmation of fact about the goods.
The seller need not be a merchant.
A conspicuous written disclaimer can exclude it without using the word "fitness."
oe: True. Actual reliance is required (cmt. 1).
True. Knowledge gained after contracting isn't enough.
Correct. This is the false statement. Fitness arises from the seller's reason to know of the purpose and of the buyer's reliance; an affirmation of fact is what creates an express warranty.
True. § 2-315 has no merchant requirement, though the warranty usually arises with merchants.
True. § 2-316(2) requires a conspicuous writing but no particular words for fitness.
topic: 4 · Implied warranties (§§ 2-314, 2-315) — Fitness: NOT correct

q: Which of the following is NOT required to create an express warranty under § 2-313?
o: The seller used a formal word such as "warrant" or "guarantee."
The seller made an affirmation of fact, a promise, a description, a sample, or a model.
The statement was more than the seller's opinion or commendation of the goods.
The statement became part of the basis of the bargain.
The affirmation or promise relates to the goods.
oe: Correct. This is not required. § 2-313(2) says formal words and a specific intention to warrant are unnecessary.
Required. One of these is the source of every express warranty.
Required. Opinion, commendation, and statements of value create no warranty (§ 2-313(2)).
Required. Each subsection of § 2-313(1) uses the basis-of-the-bargain test.
Required. § 2-313(1)(a) covers statements that relate to the goods.
topic: 3 · Express warranties (§ 2-313) — Not required for express warranty

q: Prairie Dawn buys a pair of everyday walking shoes from a shoe store. She tells the clerk only that she wants comfortable shoes for walking around town. After a week of ordinary walking, both soles split. What is her best warranty claim?
o: None, because a week of wear proves the shoes were merchantable when sold.
Breach of the implied warranty of merchantability.
None, because she didn't rely on the clerk's skill in choosing them.
Breach of express warranty, because the store sold them as "shoes."
Breach of the implied warranty of fitness, because she told the clerk she would walk in them.
oe: Soles splitting after a week of ordinary use is evidence of a defect at the time of sale.
Correct. Goods sold by a merchant must be fit for the ordinary purposes for which such goods are used (§ 2-314(2)(c)). Walking is the customary use of shoes.
Reliance matters for fitness, not merchantability. Merchantability arises from the merchant's sale alone.
The bare word "shoes" is a weak express-warranty theory. Merchantability squarely covers this defect.
Walking is the ordinary purpose of shoes, not a particular one (§ 2-315 cmt. 2). That falls under merchantability.
topic: 4 · Implied warranties (§§ 2-314, 2-315) — Ordinary purpose

q: A furniture dealer sells Abby a dining set. During the sale, the dealer says aloud, "I'm not giving you any warranty of merchantability on this set." Nothing is put in writing. Abby told the dealer she needed a table that could seat twelve and relied on his pick. Which implied warranties survive?
o: Neither, because the dealer clearly disclaimed implied warranties.
Only the implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose.
Only merchantability, because a merchantability disclaimer must be in writing.
Neither, because a consumer can never receive a fitness warranty.
Both merchantability and fitness, because disclaimers must always be written.
oe: The dealer mentioned only merchantability, and orally. That can't exclude fitness.
Correct. A merchantability disclaimer may be oral if it mentions merchantability (§ 2-316(2)). Fitness can be excluded only by a writing, so the oral statement leaves it intact.
Backwards. A merchantability disclaimer may be oral if it mentions merchantability; it's the fitness disclaimer that must be written.
Consumers routinely receive fitness warranties when § 2-315's elements are met.
Only the fitness disclaimer must be written. A merchantability disclaimer may be oral.
topic: 6 · Warranty disclaimers (§ 2-316) — Oral merchantability disclaimer

q: A seed company's contract limits the farmer's remedy to "replacement of seed reported defective within 10 days of delivery." The seed's defect, low germination, can't be discovered until weeks after planting. What is the most likely result when the farmer's crop fails?
o: The farmer gets replacement seed, which the contract promised.
The farmer gets nothing, because he didn't report the defect within 10 days.
The limited remedy fails of its essential purpose.
The farmer gets nothing, because seed is sold "as is" by usage of trade.
The farmer may recover, but only if the seller acted in bad faith.
oe: Replacement seed weeks into the season is worthless; that's why the remedy fails.
Enforcing an impossible deadline would leave the farmer with no remedy at all.
Correct. A remedy limited to a period that expires before a latent defect can be discovered deprives the buyer of a fair quantum of remedy and fails of its essential purpose (§ 2-719(2), cmt. 1).
Nothing in the facts shows such a usage of trade.
Failure of essential purpose doesn't require bad faith.
topic: 8 · Limited remedies (§ 2-719) — Latent defect, short window

q: Scooter Corp. buys a space heater from Fozzie's Appliance and puts it in the home office of its employee, Animal. The heater shorts out and burns Animal's garage. No one is hurt. Under which version of § 2-318 does Animal have a warranty claim against Fozzie's?
o: Alternative A only.
Alternatives A and B.
Alternatives B and C.
Alternative C only.
None of the above.
oe: Alternative A covers only natural persons in the buyer's family or household, or guests in its home, who are injured in person. Animal is an employee of a corporate buyer and suffered only property damage.
Both A and B require injury "in person." Animal suffered only property damage.
Alternative B requires personal injury, so it doesn't help Animal.
Correct. Alternative C extends warranties to any person reasonably expected to use, consume, or be affected by the goods who is injured by the breach, and isn't limited to personal injury.
Alternative C covers Animal.
topic: 7 · Privity & cumulation (§§ 2-317, 2-318) — § 2-318: property damage

q: Kermit agrees in November to buy a new $60,000 bass boat from a marine dealer and pays a $6,000 deposit. The contract says: "If Buyer fails to complete the purchase, Seller shall retain the deposit as liquidated damages." Boats sell slowly in winter, and the dealer's expected profit on the sale was about $7,000. Kermit backs out. What is the most likely result?
o: The dealer keeps $12,000, 20% of the price, by offsetting the balance against Kermit's other accounts.
The dealer keeps the $6,000 and may also sue Kermit for any further lost profit.
Kermit recovers all but $500, because a seller may keep only the smaller of 20% or $500.
The dealer keeps the $6,000, because the amount is reasonable in light of the anticipated harm.
Kermit recovers the full $6,000, because deposits can never be forfeited.
oe: Twenty percent is part of the § 2-718(2)(b) default, not an entitlement, and the clause liquidates damages at the $6,000 deposit.
A valid liquidated damages clause fixes the measure of damages; the dealer can't keep it and also seek more.
That default applies only when there is no valid liquidated damages term (§ 2-718(2)(b)). Here there is one.

Correct. Forfeiture of a down payment is frequently enforced when the amount is a reasonable liquidation (§ 2-718(1), (2)(a)). A 10% deposit, close to the expected lost profit on a hard-to-resell boat, qualifies.
Deposits can be forfeited when they reasonably liquidate the seller's damages.
topic: 2 · Liquidated damages (§ 2-718) — Forfeited boat deposit

q: A sawmill buys a log debarker under a contract with two separate clauses: an exclusive repair-or-replace remedy and an exclusion of consequential damages. The seller's repairs fail for months, and the limited remedy fails of its essential purpose. The state's courts follow the minority (dependent) approach. The sawmill sues for profits lost during the downtime. What is the most likely result?
o: Lost profits only if the exclusion clause was not printed conspicuously.
No lost profits, because the exclusion is tested on its own and isn't unconscionable between merchants.
Nothing at all, because repair or replacement was the sawmill's exclusive remedy.
No lost profits, because consequential damages can never be recovered for purely commercial losses.
The sawmill may recover its lost profits, because under the dependent approach the exclusion falls along with the failed remedy.
oe: § 2-719 has no conspicuousness requirement, under either approach.
That is the majority (independent) approach. This state follows the dependent approach.
When an exclusive remedy fails of its essential purpose, the buyer may resort to Code remedies (§ 2-719(2)).
Lost profits are classic consequential damages (§ 2-715(2)(a)). They are excludable by agreement, but not barred by law.

Correct. Under the dependent approach, a seller that fails to deliver the limited remedy can't keep the benefit of the consequential-damages exclusion; both fall together. (The majority, independent approach would test the exclusion separately for unconscionability.)
topic: 8 · Limited remedies (§ 2-719) — Dependent approach

q: Which of the following statements about liquidated damages under § 2-718 is NOT correct?
o: A clause is enforceable only if the actual harm later proves hard to measure.
Nothing in § 2-718 requires the clause to be conspicuous.
The clause may state a fixed sum or a formula for computing damages.
Damages for breach by either the buyer or the seller may be liquidated in the agreement.
A term fixing unreasonably large liquidated damages is void as a penalty.
oe: Correct. This is the false statement. Difficulty of proof is one factor in judging reasonableness; it isn't a condition that the actual harm turn out hard to measure. A clause reasonable in light of anticipated harm can be enforced.
True. Conspicuousness is a § 2-316 requirement for some disclaimers, not for liquidated damages.
True. Either form is permitted.
True. § 2-718(1) applies to "breach by either party."
True. That is the last sentence of § 2-718(1).
topic: 2 · Liquidated damages (§ 2-718) — LD rules: NOT correct

q: Which of the following is true of a delegation of performance under § 2-210?
o: Absent a contrary agreement or a substantial interest, the other party's consent isn't required.
The delegating party remains liable if the delegate's performance is defective.
A delegate who never agreed to assume the duty isn't liable to the other party for failing to perform.
All of the above.
None of the above.
oe: True, but not the only true statement (§ 2-210(1)).
True, but not the only true statement (§ 2-210(1)).
True, but not the only true statement. A delegate becomes bound to the obligee only by assuming the duty.
Correct. Each statement is accurate. Delegation needs no consent by default, never releases the delegator, and binds the delegate only if it assumes the duty.
Each of A, B, and C is a correct statement of the law.
topic: 1 · Assignment & delegation (§ 2-210) — Delegation: all true

q: Herry's contract to sell 400 trophies to a youth league says: "Neither party may assign this contract." After delivering the trophies, Herry assigns his right to the $6,000 price to a finance company, which notifies the league. The league argues the assignment violates the contract. Which statement is most accurate?
o: It is effective, because the clause bars only delegation, and Herry delegated nothing.
The assignment is effective, but the league may cancel the contract for Herry's breach.
The assignment is ineffective unless the league consented in writing.
The assignment is ineffective, because the clause expressly bars assigning the contract.
The assignment is effective only because the finance company is a merchant.
oe: Correct. § 2-210(4) reads the clause as barring delegation of performance only. Herry has already performed and transferred only his right to payment, which is effective (see also § 9-406(d)).
Assigning the right to payment doesn't breach a clause that bars only delegation, and § 9-406(d) says it isn't a default.
Consent isn't required to assign a right to payment.
Under § 2-210(4) that wording reaches only delegation of duties, and Herry assigned only a right.
The assignee's status is irrelevant. The result follows from § 2-210(4) and § 9-406(d).
topic: 1 · Assignment & delegation (§ 2-210) — Ban on assigning payment rights
